defaults.permitted_development: In Scotland, ancillary family accommodation may sometimes be achieved through ordinary extension rules or an incidental outbuilding, but a true self-contained annexe should not be assumed to be permitted development and will often need planning permission.

rules.height_rules: Where a detached ancillary building relies on ordinary Scottish outbuilding rights, keep within the Class 3A limits: eaves up to 3m, up to 4m overall and no more than 2.5m overall for any part within 1m of the boundary.
rules.depth_rules: There is no separate annexe depth allowance. Attached accommodation must stay within the normal extension rules, while detached space must stay within the relevant curtilage limits and still read as ancillary rather than a second home.
rules.boundary_rules: A detached incidental building cannot be forward of an elevation fronting a road, and close-boundary siting also affects whether the structure still looks ancillary or starts to read as a separate planning unit.
rules.roof_rules: If the proposal relies on ancillary-building rights, keep it single storey and visually subordinate. Terrace-style roofs, overt upper-storey accommodation and dominant house-like forms usually move the scheme outside the ordinary Scottish route.
rules.materials_rules: If permission is granted for annexe accommodation, conditions often keep the use ancillary to the main dwelling. Materials, servicing, entrances and window layout should reinforce that relationship rather than suggest a freestanding new house.

rules.permitted_development: The critical Scottish distinction is between ancillary accommodation tied to the main house and a separate planning unit. Once the space functions as self-contained living accommodation, a planning application is usually needed.

rules.height_rules: Detached ancillary space can only borrow the ordinary Scottish outbuilding height rules while it remains incidental: eaves up to 3m, an overall height up to 4m and no more than 2.5m overall near the boundary.
rules.depth_rules: Instead of a dedicated annexe projection right, the Scottish route depends on form and use: extensions follow the normal house rules, while detached structures must stay within the usual ancillary-building limits and remain clearly ancillary.
rules.boundary_rules: Where annexe-style space sits tight to a boundary, the authority will usually look at both physical impact and independence. Separate access, services and a self-contained layout point away from the ordinary householder route.
rules.roof_rules: Roof form matters because it can make the structure read like a second dwelling. A simple, subordinate single-storey roof is much safer than a dominant or house-like design.
rules.materials_rules: The external treatment should show that the accommodation belongs to the same dwellinghouse plot. Separate-house cues such as autonomous servicing, an independent entrance arrangement and overtly domestic detailing can make the proposal harder to justify.

rules.permitted_development: Scottish annexe proposals need to be treated cautiously. Householder rights may cover attached ancillary space or an incidental garden building, but they do not normally allow a separate self-contained residence within the plot.

rules.height_rules: If the proposal depends on Scottish ancillary-building rights, keep to the standard envelope: eaves no higher than 3m, an overall maximum of 4m and a 2.5m overall cap where any part sits within 1m of the boundary.
rules.depth_rules: Depth is not the real Scottish annexe test. An attached scheme must satisfy the ordinary extension rules, while a detached building must remain within the curtilage and still be genuinely ancillary in use.
rules.boundary_rules: Boundary and road-facing siting matter for both scale and independence of use. Detached buildings with their own facilities, access and close-boundary siting are harder to defend as ordinary incidental development.
rules.roof_rules: A detached ancillary building should stay low-key if you want to remain within the normal Scottish outbuilding route. Roof terraces, upper floors and house-like forms often indicate that a full planning application is the safer route.
rules.materials_rules: When permission is sought for annexe accommodation, authorities often keep the use tied to the main house. Design choices such as entrances, window pattern, materials and servicing should support that subordinate relationship.

rules.height_rules: Detached ancillary space can only borrow the ordinary Scottish outbuilding height rules while it remains incidental: eaves up to 3m, an overall height up to 4m and no more than 2.5m overall near the boundary.
rules.depth_rules: Instead of a dedicated annexe projection right, the Scottish route depends on form and use: extensions follow the normal house rules, while detached structures must stay within the usual ancillary-building limits and remain clearly ancillary.
rules.boundary_rules: Where annexe-style space sits tight to a boundary, the authority will usually look at both physical impact and independence. Separate access, services and a self-contained layout point away from the ordinary householder route.
rules.roof_rules: Roof form matters because it can make the structure read like a second dwelling. A simple, subordinate single-storey roof is much safer than a dominant or house-like design.
rules.materials_rules: The external treatment should show that the accommodation belongs to the same dwellinghouse plot. Separate-house cues such as autonomous servicing, an independent entrance arrangement and overtly domestic detailing can make the proposal harder to justify.

rules.permitted_development: In Scotland, ancillary family accommodation may sometimes be achieved through ordinary extension rules or an incidental outbuilding, but a true self-contained annexe should not be assumed to be permitted development and will often need planning permission.

rules.height_rules: Where a detached ancillary building relies on ordinary Scottish outbuilding rights, keep within the Class 3A limits: eaves up to 3m, up to 4m overall and no more than 2.5m overall for any part within 1m of the boundary.
rules.depth_rules: There is no separate annexe depth allowance. Attached accommodation must stay within the normal extension rules, while detached space must stay within the relevant curtilage limits and still read as ancillary rather than a second home.
rules.boundary_rules: A detached incidental building cannot be forward of an elevation fronting a road, and close-boundary siting also affects whether the structure still looks ancillary or starts to read as a separate planning unit.
rules.roof_rules: If the proposal relies on ancillary-building rights, keep it single storey and visually subordinate. Terrace-style roofs, overt upper-storey accommodation and dominant house-like forms usually move the scheme outside the ordinary Scottish route.
rules.materials_rules: If permission is granted for annexe accommodation, conditions often keep the use ancillary to the main dwelling. Materials, servicing, entrances and window layout should reinforce that relationship rather than suggest a freestanding new house.
